principles: Shared lifecycle, health, governance, finality and direction semantics are canonical.
Cross-dApp dependencies resolve through shared interfaces and registries where practical.
Names and identity are presentation/credential layers, not ownership truth.
Canonical asset identity never relies on ticker symbol alone.
Security-sensitive integrations fail closed on inactive, paused, stale, unsupported or unhealthy dependencies.
Historical object identity remains immutable across upgrades.
Major version changes require explicit migration/review.

core_security_semantics.capabilities: bounded operational authority distinct from governance and ownership
core_security_semantics.custody: accounting authority and release authority are separate; custody positions expose deposited/committed/released/available amounts
core_security_semantics.genesis_initialization: predeploys expose initialization state and genesis configuration hash because constructor execution cannot be assumed for genesis-inserted runtime code
core_security_semantics.migration: historical implementation identity is preserved; registry pointer changes do not rewrite provenance
core_security_semantics.system_safety: NORMAL/DEGRADED/HALTED/RECOVERY are distinct from local component pause; actions declare safe-operation class

freeze_rules.major: semantic change requires new major interface version, migration plan and at least G3 review; G4 if constitutional invariant changes

security_invariants: Delegated authority never implies ownership or unrestricted custody.
Accounting authority and custody/release authority are distinct.
Genesis configuration must be introspectable and hash-verifiable.
System safety state is distinct from local pause state.
Security-sensitive dependencies fail closed when inactive, unhealthy, stale, unsupported or code-hash mismatched.
Application signatures are domain-separated and replay-resistant.
Canonical asset identity never relies on ticker symbol alone.
Dust and rounding effects are explicit and never silently discarded.
External dependencies are registry-addressed and lifecycle-controlled.
